title: Planetary Nebula PuWe 1
caption: The planetary nebula PuWe 1, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab) & H. Schweiker (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This wide-field image shows PuWe 1 in the constellation Lynx, one of the biggest and faintest planetary nebulae known. Despite the name, a planetary nebula has nothing to do with planets: the term dates from early telescopes, when some of these round glowing clouds looked a little like planetary discs.
PuWe 1 formed when a red giant star shed its outer layers as it neared its death. What remains of the star's core, a white dwarf, energises the expelled gas and makes it glow.

Its faintness comes from its size. As a planetary nebula expands, its gas moves further and further from the white dwarf that powers it, and it grows dimmer. Over time such nebulae spread out and fade, eventually mixing into the gas between the stars.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and oxygen [O III] in blue.
